rationale: A wins because it does the adult PR thing: it separates a usable news angle from the proof needed to survive a reporter's second question. Its line, "Whatnot hit $3B in sales — so what do its sellers actually take home?", turns the missing take-rate into a real beat-shaped question; B's "Whatnot Moves Into Fashion and Electronics, Squeezing Resale's Incumbents" invents a competitive knife fight the update never gave it. B has bones, but A is the set a founder can act on without accidentally pitching fan fiction.
gaps_in_A: "Whatnot is betting US shoppers behave like Asia's — the data so far says they don't" overstates the supplied facts. The update says Asia is far larger; it does not provide data proving US shoppers reject the behavior.

"the first hard data point that the format scales past collectors" is not proven by the $3B number unless Whatnot can break out fashion/electronics from collectibles. A flags this later, but the angle still leans on it.

"Whatnot hit $3B in sales — so what do its sellers actually take home?" is a strong question, not yet a pitchable data story. Without take-rate or seller-earnings distribution, the reporter has to do the hard part.
gaps_in_B: "The $3B GMV" treats sales as GMV before proving it. B then asks whether the number is GMV or net revenue, which means it knows the claim is unresolved and says it anyway.
"since TikTok Shop's US launch" is an external news peg not in the update. Maybe relevant, maybe not, but in this blind task it is imported scenery.
"Squeezing Resale's Incumbents" plus "Poshmark, Depop, and eBay" invents the opponent list. The update names no competitors and gives no overlap data.

"someone who goes live repeatedly each week selling trading cards or sneakers as a primary income source" adds color the update does not support. No sneakers, no full-time seller profile, no earnings proof.
